claims.text: The target material is a single-phase high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
Such a Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy can be prepared by conventional arc melting or powder metallurgy while retaining the specified single-phase state.
The intervention is a uniform, conformal, approximately 100 nm Al2O3 coating deposited by atomic layer deposition.
An oxidation-resistant coating will suppress high-temperature surface oxidation of the alloy.
The coating will suppress oxygen, nitrogen, and other impurity ingress into the alloy.
The alumina layer acts as a barrier to impurity penetration into the alloy surface and grain boundaries.
Reducing impurity penetration will reduce oxidation-driven phase segregation.
Reducing impurity penetration will reduce precipitate-free-zone formation at grain boundaries.
Oxygen and nitrogen interstitials can promote phase segregation during high-temperature aging.
Impurity-associated phase evolution and depletion of interstitial solutes can cause progressive softening during thermal aging.
The coating will preserve the alloy's pristine single-phase microstructure during elevated-temperature exposure.
Preserving the single-phase microstructure will mitigate impurity-induced softening.
The coating will maintain dislocation mobility conducive to both high yield strength and ductility.
Coated specimens will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than uncoated specimens.
Coated specimens will have greater elevated-temperature ductility than uncoated specimens.
Coated specimens will exhibit less surface oxidation and grain-boundary degradation than uncoated specimens.
An uncoated Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy is prone to oxidation and impurity pickup that degrade its high-temperature mechanical performance.
The proposed applicability range is 600–1000 °C in air or mildly oxidizing atmospheres for single-phase Ti–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Evidence from other high-temperature high-entropy alloys links interstitial impurities to aging-induced segregation and softening and identifies anti-oxidation coatings as needed for service in air.
The magnitude of improvement and the long-term adhesion and stability of ALD alumina under thermal cycling are not established.
